transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Maya Chen (AE), Ravi Patel (SE), Clara Ruiz (SRE)
Attendees (Lyra): Daniel Park (Head of Platform), Asha Kapoor (Lead ML Eng), Tom Nguyen (Network Eng)
Link: shared deck and bench: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/lyra-latency-2026 (slide + raw csv)

Summary:
Redwood-led latency / tail analysis focused on p95/p99 spikes seen in Lyra's chat assistant traffic. Primary hypotheses: inter-region VPC hops + KV cache hot-shards + quantization path mismatches causing amplified tail under burst. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming decoding tail behavior and failover/buffering policies for Dedicated vs Private. Agreed next steps include sharing raw logs, planning on-prem pilot checks, and running targeted KV heatmap tests.

Topics covered:
- p95/p99 characterization and measurement methods
- streaming vs non-streaming tail differences with small prefix vs long context
- KV cache hotkey detection + eviction behavior
- batching latency SLO tradeoffs and queueing under burst
- quantization mismatch regressions and runtime kernel fallback
- multi-region VPC hops, hairpinning, and eBPF-based tracing
- failover policies: canary -> fallback -> degrade to smaller model

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): ok everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time, we wanted to walk through the tail-amplification pattern you sent and run through a couple root-cause hypotheses, quick intros?
[00:00:18] Daniel Park (Lyra): yeah hi, Daniel here, we own platform infra, we saw p99s spike to ~1.2s on certain bursts and it's impacting UX, so high priority.
[00:00:27] Asha Kapoor (Lyra): Asha, ML lead, we've instrumented model latency and we see most token lat spikes on warm caches during heavy concurrent sessions.
[00:00:34] Ravi Patel (Redwood SE): thanks, ok first Q: are those calls streaming or non-streaming? meaning are you using chunked streaming from Redwood or waiting for full response?
[00:00:42] Tom Nguyen (Lyra): mostly streaming, but some internal endpoints call non-stream to compose multiple instructions server-side, so mix.
[00:00:48] [00:01:02] Clara Ruiz (Redwood SRE): quick note: streaming adds more network RTT sensitivity per token, non-streaming can mask per-token jitters but increases tail when generation stalls.
[00:01:20] Daniel: correct, that matches our observation — when we switch to non-stream for a batch job the p95 improves but p99 worsens for interactive flows.
[00:01:32] Ravi: ok, so one big suspect is multi-region VPC hairpinning. Tom, do requests route across regions or originate in same AZ most of the time?
[00:01:41] Tom: most traffic origin is in us-east-1, but for redundancy we have a secondary region eu-west-1 that will occasionally take requests (DNS-weighted failover), sometimes we see a hop to eu-west then back to us-east for DB reads (ugh).
[00:01:55] [00:02:10] Maya: that hairpin is classic tail multiplier — an extra 50-120ms RTT sometimes stacked with kernel-level serialization. Are you doing VPC peering or transit gateway?
[00:02:19] Tom: transit gateway, NAT in the middle for some of the egress, we suspect some MTU or reassembly causing rare packet stalls.
[00:02:29] Asha: we also saw a correlation between certain user sessions that hit a KV hotkey pattern — similar prompts hitting same cache slot. Does Redwood's KV cache have hotspot mitigation?
[00:02:41] Ravi: good q — the K/V cache (we sometimes call it K V cache in docs) has LRU but we also have sharding by key hash; if one shard becomes hot you'll see serialization on that worker. We can enable a hotkey splitter or replicate hot shards; Clara will show heatmap examples.
[00:02:58] Clara: (screen share) here's a heatmap from your sample window — you can see a single cache shard accounting for 37% of lookups during the spike window. There are serialization waits visible at 10-30ms each, stacking across tokens.
[00:03:15] Daniel: that's helpful, so what are the remediation patterns? shard replication, client-side bucketing?
[00:03:22] Ravi: replicate hot shard async, add jitter on client keys, or front a small consistent-hash ring that rotates. Also we can do prefix-caching for frequent prompt prefixes — that reduces both compute and cache lookups.
[00:03:34] [00:03:50] Maya: another angle is quantization path mismatch — Lyra mentioned you run both q8 and int4 variants?
[00:03:56] Asha: we tried int4 to save cost but observed occasional slowdowns where the runtime falls back to fp16 kernels for some ops, causing per-token latency to spike.
[00:04:07] Ravi: that happens when operator kernels aren't available for that specific layer shape on your hardware. The runtime tries a fallback path which is correct but slower. We track kernel fallback counts in the dashboard — you should look for 'fallback-exec' spikes.
[00:04:20] Tom: any way to avoid that during bursts?
[00:04:24] Ravi: either pin to a model variant with validated kernel coverage or enable proactive kernel compilation at deploy time, or use Redwood Optimize suggestions which recommend quant+kernel profiles per workload.
[00:04:35] [00:04:58] Daniel: streaming vs non-streaming — can you explain why streaming seems to have worse p99 even though median is lower?
[00:05:05] Clara: streaming exposes per-token tail — imagine each token is another network roundtrip or chunk. If there's intermittent jitter on the path (like in your hairpin), the last few tokens' delays amplify p99 even if p50 is great. Non-streaming aggregates but then the entire response can be stuck behind a slow tail during generation, so you see different tail shapes.
[00:05:25] Asha: so for our chat UX we prefer streaming for perceived responsiveness; how do we protect p99?
[00:05:31] Ravi: set token-level timeouts and graceful fallback: if streaming stalls for >X ms, stream a partial cached prefix and switch to non-stream for remaining tokens, or fallback to smaller model variant for completion. That's how you maintain perceived latency while bounding tail.
[00:05:45] [00:06:10] Tom: is there precedent for hybrid — start streaming, if you detect KV hotshard throttling do non-stream for that session?
[00:06:18] Maya: yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing: you can define a per-route policy that says on KV-latency>Y ms switch to fallback-route, or prefer dedicated pool. We can demo rule config in Console later.
[00:06:31] Daniel: about Dedicated vs Private — from infra perspective, we were thinking Private (VPC) to reduce hairpins. Would that remove the transit gateway issues?
[00:06:40] Clara: Private removes the public transit path but you still need cross-region peering design; if you keep control-plane in our cloud and data plane in your VPC you still can encounter egress routes. On-prem gives most control but requires more integration.
[00:06:55] Asha: any performance delta between Dedicated GPUs in Redwood vs our on-prem instances?
[00:07:01] Ravi: Dedicated in our regions are tuned with our kernel selection and batching stack; typically similar raw throughput to equivalent on-prem GPUs, but our autoscaler and prefix/KV cache are co-designed. On-prem depends on your stack and kernel builds — miscompiled kernels can cause the fallback penalties we saw.
[00:07:16] [00:07:45] Maya: we also discussed batching: large batches improve throughput but increase queueing delay for first token. Under bursty interactive traffic you want small batch sizes and continuous batching window tuned to SLO. Have you tuned batching?
[00:07:58] Asha: we left batching at default and saw queue spikes; what window should we use?
[00:08:05] Ravi: for <200ms p95 SLOs we suggest max-batch 8 with 8-12ms batching window and adaptive abort for high-urgency session types. Also enable preemptive batching for VIP tokens.
[00:08:17] Tom: you mentioned kernel selection — are there metrics we can surface to detect fallback early?
[00:08:23] Clara: yes, kernel-fallback-count, op-latency-distribution, and quant-failure-rate streams. We can ship an alert rule that triggers when fallback-rate > 0.5% over 5m.
[00:08:35] [00:08:50] Daniel: about KV eviction — what TTL / capacity strategies do you recommend for chat contexts?
[00:08:56] Ravi: TTLs depend on context reuse, but we recommend LRU with priority bands: keep most recent user contexts and replicate hot items. Also consider a small client-side prefix cache to reduce server lookups for high-frequency prompts.
[00:09:10] Asha: okay, let's talk about measuring p99 correctly — we use synthetic load & distributed tracing but maybe measurement is biased by sampling.
[00:09:19] Maya: ensure you capture end-to-end spans (client ingress -> model token completions) and measure both server-side decode time and network e2e. p99 of server decode vs p99 of e2e can differ a lot. Also use quantile sketches and keep raw tail buckets for postmortem.
[00:09:34] [00:09:50] Tom: we can add eBPF or packet capture in staging to confirm reassembly stalls. Will Redwood need access?
[00:09:57] Clara: yes for root-cause we may ask for staged pcap logs or eBPF traces. We'll provide minimal guidance and a safe collection script.
[00:10:05] Daniel: any quick wins we can apply before the pilot?
[00:10:09] Ravi: enable hotkey replication, reduce per-shard max queue depth, and pin model to the validated quant profile. That should reduce stacked waits. Also lower streaming chunk size to reduce per-chunk RTT sensitivity.
[00:10:22] Asha: is there a cost tradeoff? smaller chunks mean more packets, more overhead.
[00:10:27] Ravi: yes; it's a latency vs cost tradeoff. We'll show numbers in the benchmark sheet for network I/O vs p99 improvement.
[00:10:36] [00:11:00] Maya: ok let's walk through the sample logs you sent — (Ravi) can you narrate heatmap and flame charts?
[00:11:06] Ravi: sure, here is a flame chart from one of the p99 traces: DNS lookup 5ms, TCP handshake 12ms (this is the hairpin roundtrip), token-decode slice 20-40ms but for the slowest tokens we see a kernel-fallback op adding 120ms. Combine that with KV shard lock waits 25-30ms and you get the amplified p99.
[00:11:28] Daniel: wow that chain explains the 1.2s p99.
[00:11:31] [00:11:45] Tom: for the transit gateway we do see reassemble warnings — likely MTU mismatch, we'll check.
[00:11:50] Clara: once you fix MTU you'll likely remove some stalls; still we should replicate hotkeys and adjust batching.
[00:11:58] Maya: for pilot scope: run a 2-week controlled load test with Redwood Dedicated from us-east and a Private staging in your VPC and compare p50/p95/p99, plus kernel-fallback counters and KV heatmaps. Agreed?
[00:12:12] Daniel: yes, sounds good.
[00:12:15] Asha: timeline?
[00:12:18] Maya: we propose start week of 2026-12-20, planning call before that.
[00:12:22] [00:12:40] (cross-talk)
[00:12:44] Ravi: one more note on failover policies — our Console supports automatic fallback to smaller model or dedicated pool on high-p95; we can route sessions by tag so VIPs always hit smaller latency tail pools.
[00:12:57] Tom: can we enforce RBAC on those route rules?
[00:13:02] Clara: yes SSO/SAML + RBAC for route edits, and we keep an audit trail. We'll send the audit log retention options.
[00:13:10] Daniel: ok can you summarize actions and owners?
[00:13:15] Maya: sure — Ravi will export heatmaps and kernel-fallback CSVs (due 12/14), Tom will confirm network topology and share eBPF/pcap (due 12/16), Maya to send pilot SOW + pricing + compliance docs (due 12/13).
[00:13:27] (brief pause)
[00:13:40] Asha: quick Q on quantization: if kernel fallback appears during pilot can we disable int4 globally for their pool?
[00:13:47] Ravi: yes you can set model-variant constraints for a pool. It's an easy toggle in deployment config.
[00:13:52] [00:14:10] Daniel: any competitor risk? Anthropic was mentioned as offering single-region endpoints — but we prefer Redwood's fallback and observability features.
[00:14:20] Maya: ok we'll send a short competitive note.
[00:14:25] (closing)
[00:14:32] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll capture next steps in CRM and share meeting notes. Expect email with attachments in next 48 hours.
[00:14:41] Daniel: thanks, good session.
